article_title: How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing
citation: Sovrano Francesco, Ashley Kevin, Brusilovsky Peter Leonid, Vitali Fabio. (2024). How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00399-w
title: YAI4Edu: a pipeline that converts static e-books into interactive intelligent textbooks with open-ended questioning and overviewing
description: YAI4Edu is an extension of YAI4Hu that automatically transforms static educative e-books in PDF, XML or HTML format into interactive intelligent textbooks. Interaction is given by "i) word glosses that can be clicked to open an overview; ii) a special kind of search box that allows the reader to get answers to any open-ended English question." It extracts a knowledge graph of template-triplets formatted as RDF from a collection of texts and retrieves answers via embedding similarity using a MiniLM-based model. Source code and anonymized evaluation data are released under MIT license at https://github.com/Francesco-Sovrano/YAI4Edu.
requirements: A collection of texts integrating the textbook (e.g., an encyclopedia) from which to extract the knowledge graph
Hyper-parameters for the Intelligent Explanation Generator (k=10, p=.57, L=50, s=.95, q=4, a=2 in the case study)
constraints: The extracted knowledge graph is imperfect because of the adopted extraction procedure and may contain mistakes from wrongly identified grammatical dependencies
target_learners: University students in an interdisciplinary legal analytics and AI course
target_learning_goals: Learning how to write a legal memorandum in the U.S. legal system
examples: Applied to 22 textbook pages, 5,407 legal-encyclopedia web pages, and 11,198 BVA legal cases, producing an interactive annotated version of the textbook
key_sources: Sovrano Francesco, Ashley Kevin, Brusilovsky Peter Leonid, Vitali Fabio. (2024). How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00399-w

article_title: Computing With Words for Student Strategy Evaluation in an Examination
citation: Gupta, P. K., and Muhuri, P. K. (2019). Computing with words for student strategy evaluation in an examination. Granular Computing 4, no. 2, 167-184.
title: Yager's three-block model of computing with words: translation, manipulation and retranslation
description: The article presents the general CWW methodology it follows, attributed to Yager: any CWW system takes linguistic data as input and output and performs three steps. As the article puts it, "in Yager's CWW methodology, there are three building blocks: translation, manipulation and retranslation." Translation converts words into mathematical representations using fuzzy sets because computers process numeric information; manipulation aggregates the numeric information to generate recommendations; retranslation converts the aggregated numeric result back into linguistic form because humans naturally prefer words. The different CWW methodologies (extension principle, symbolic method, 2-tuple, Per-C) differ principally in how they represent the semantics of linguistic information through fuzzy sets.
requirements: Linguistic term sets whose words are represented as fuzzy sets so that translation and retranslation between linguistic and numeric form is possible
target_learning_goals: processing linguistic evaluations of student performance
examples: The paper's Algorithms 1-3 for the extension principle, symbolic method and 2-tuple approaches each follow the translate-aggregate-retranslate structure, as does Per-C's Encoder-CWW engine-Decoder chain
key_sources: Gupta, P. K., and Muhuri, P. K. (2019). Computing with words for student strategy evaluation in an examination. Granular Computing 4, no. 2, 167-184. https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.00868

article_title: On the Nature of Programming Exercises
citation: Alberto Simões and Ricardo Queirós. (2020). On the Nature of Programming Exercises. OpenAccess Series in Informatics, ICPEC 2020. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.14476
title: YAPeXIL exercise format supporting varied programming exercise types
description: YAPeXIL is a programming exercise serialization format, based on PExIL, that changed the serialization format to JSON and supports "different types of programming exercises such as solution improvement, bug fix, gap filling, block sorting, and spot the bug". Like other formats, it follows a structure of an XML manifest referring to resources such as problem statements, images, input/output test files, validators and solution implementations, and allows inclusion of metadata, instructions, tests and tools.
requirements: Exercise formats must represent metadata, instructions, tests and tools to serve discovery, presentation and automatic assessment
target_learners: computer science course students using programming exercises in training environments
target_learning_goals: practice on varied programming exercise types
examples: The paper names KATTIS, FreeProblemSet, Mooshak Exchange Format, PExIL and YAPeXIL as notable exercise representation formats
key_sources: Alberto Simões and Ricardo Queirós. (2020). On the Nature of Programming Exercises. OpenAccess Series in Informatics, ICPEC 2020. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.14476
